title: Small Talk
description: The questions every visitor gets asked, and how to answer them: where you're from, how long you've been here, whether you like Indonesia, and the everyday greetings Mau ke mana? and Sudah makan?

phrases.registerNotes: Asal is origin, and -nya avoids choosing a word for 'you'. You'll also hear the short Dari mana? and, to someone older, Bapak asalnya dari mana?
phrases.cultureNote: Visitors are asked this all the time, by drivers, vendors and neighbours. It's friendly curiosity, and the chat often moves on to whether you're married and have children.

phrases.registerNotes: Selandia Baru is New Zealand. Adding your city helps: Saya dari Auckland.
phrases.pitfallNote: There's no word for 'am': dari (from) is enough.

phrases.english: How long have you been in Indonesia?
phrases.registerNotes: Answer Sudah dua minggu (two weeks now) or Baru tiga hari (only three days). The next question is often Berapa lama lagi? (How much longer?).
A favourite question for visitors, often followed by Suka makanan Indonesia? (Do you like Indonesian food?) and Bisa makan pedas? (Can you eat spicy food?).
Sekali after a word means very. To be specific: Saya suka sekali makanannya (I love the food).
Sedang marks something going on now; with friends, Aku lagi belajar bahasa Indonesia.
phrases.pitfallNote: The language is bahasa Indonesia. Bahasa on its own just means 'language', and Indonesia on its own is the country.
phrases.cultureNote: Even a few words get a warm reaction, often Wah, pintar (Oh, clever) or Sudah lancar (You're fluent already), however basic your Indonesian is.

phrases.english: I only speak a little so far.
phrases.registerNotes: Baru (only, so far) sounds modest and hopeful. Sedikit-sedikit (a little bit) is the usual short answer to Bisa bahasa Indonesia?
phrases.pitfallNote: Speaking a language is just bisa (can): Bisa bahasa Inggris? means Do you speak English? There's no need for a verb like bicara.

phrases.registerNotes: From neighbours and people you pass, often with your title: Mau ke mana, Mbak?
phrases.cultureNote: It's a greeting, like 'how's it going?', not nosiness. Nobody expects details, and a vague answer is perfectly polite.

phrases.registerNotes: The stock vague answer to Mau ke mana? Others: Ke depan (just up the road), Ke pasar (to the market), Pulang (home).
Asked when someone sees you coming back. Answer just as briefly: Dari pasar (from the market), Dari kantor (from work).
phrases.pitfallNote: The same words can mean 'where are you from?'. If you're walking home with shopping, they mean where you've been.

phrases.registerNotes: Answer Sudah (yes, already) or Belum (not yet). Sudah, terima kasih is always safe.
phrases.pitfallNote: Don't answer ya or tidak: sudah and belum are the yes and no to any Sudah …? question.
phrases.cultureNote: A friendly greeting, especially around mealtimes. It shows care rather than inviting you to eat.
